title: Holy Week's middle days
hook: Monday to Wednesday: the fig tree, the temple, the anointing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosanna: coats and branches on the road, and a crowd singing a psalm. Your line was blessed is he who comes. Who did you greet that way? Day one thousand twenty-nine.

So what happened on the Monday? Between the shouting on the road and the supper on Thursday, there are a few days that are easy to skip. Mark sets three strange scenes among them. A fig tree covered in leaves and bare of fruit. Tables tipped over in the temple courts, coins rolling on the stones. And a dinner in Bethany where a woman breaks open a jar of perfume and pours it over Jesus's head while the guests stare. Tradition spreads these scenes across the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week. They feel like the held breath before everything happens. Today, Holy Week's middle days.

First, the tree. Jesus is hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing on it. Mark even adds that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus speaks to it, and the next morning it has withered from the roots. It's a hard little scene to read. Notice where Mark puts it: the tree comes before the temple scene and the withering comes after, so each frames the other. Some readers hear in it a warning about any religious life, their own included, that's all leaves and no fruit. Second, the temple. Jesus drives out the people buying and selling and overturns the money tables, and he quotes the prophets of Israel to do it. In the King James: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." Of all nations. Some readers hear him defending the temple's own calling, in the words of its own scriptures. Third, the jar. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly ointment over his head. Some at the table are indignant: what a waste. Jesus says, let her alone, and then: "She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying." He reads her gift as something the others hadn't seen yet: a burial anointing, ahead of time. Right after, Mark says, Judas goes to the chief priests. In some places Wednesday is called Spy Wednesday for that reason. Three scenes, and each one is quiet in its own way. A tree that says nothing. A courtyard cleared. A room full of perfume.
screen: `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean one room. For now, start with one corner of the room you're in. A shelf, a desk, the space by the bed. Pick up what's on the floor. Straighten what's crooked. Put one thing back where it lives. Go slowly, and breathe while you do it. The temple was cleared. The dinner room was filled with something costly. Either way, a space got ready for what was coming. If you pray, you can do this in silence as an offering. If you don't, just notice how the room changes when there's room in it. The bell holds the time.
Alabaster. The jar of costly ointment a woman broke open over Jesus's head at Bethany, one of three quiet scenes in Holy Week's middle days.

Your line: the quiet before. This week ran from Patrick's breastplate and Joseph's silence, through Mary's yes and going home, to an opened tomb and a road of branches. Today, do one small unseen job before the busy part begins. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some churches hold daily services on the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week, reading the Gospel scenes of these days; some households use them to clean and prepare for Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: the quiet days of Holy Week, when nothing much happens.
what it means: a withered tree, a cleared courtyard, and a woman who anoints him before anyone else understands.
what a scholar hears: Mark sets the temple scene between the two halves of the fig-tree story (Mark 11:12–21), so each one frames the other.
recall: mocked of the wise men, exceeding wroth

notes: Week end (days 1023–1029): the carry looks back at the week (Patrick, Joseph, Annunciation, Mothering Sunday, Lazarus Saturday, Palm Sunday). Day 1026 (Mothering Sunday) had no script on disk when this was written; the review of 1027 used the index.
Claims rule: Mark gives no weekdays; the assignment of scenes to Monday–Wednesday is attributed to 'tradition', following the outline. 'Spy Wednesday' attributed to 'some places'. Confirm.

The temple scene is framed as Jesus defending the temple's calling in the words of Israel's prophets, not as a judgment on Judaism. The fig tree reading is offered as 'some readers', turned inward. Confirm fairness.

Editor pass: the claim that the woman at Bethany 'understood' (not in Mark) is now Jesus's reading of her gift; practice no longer clears and wipes a surface, so it doesn't duplicate tomorrow's 'clear a table completely'.
Audit pass: 'Mark fills them with three scenes' overstated (Mark 11–13 also hold long teaching); the reading of the temple scene as defending its calling is now attributed to some readers.
